claims.text: A 38-year-old man with a history of allergic rhinitis had seven episodes of anaphylaxis at home, one progressing to anaphylactic shock. He denied medication use, specific food ingestion or Hymenoptera stings before the episodes. Initial evaluation in an allergist's office found a baseline serum tryptase of 4.10 μg/L and negative food skin tests with an appropriate positive histamine control.

claims.text: He was referred to the authors' unit, where detailed re-questioning linked the reactions to periods when his children received penicillin therapy and identified two triggers: licking a child's spoon with amoxicillin syrup traces and drinking from a glass with crushed amoxicillin tablet traces. Table 1 lists itching, angioedema, dyspnea, vomiting and loss of consciousness, acute tryptase not measured, oral corticosteroids for one reaction and none for the other, and resolution in a few hours.
